prize_parts.citation: For determining the atomic structure of nitrogenase and its iron-molybdenum cofactor, revealing how biology activates dinitrogen

statement.case_for: I keep nitrogenase as a single-part prize, but I have narrowed it. The crystallographic work of Rees on the MoFe protein and the FeMo-cofactor, and Einsle's atomic-resolution identification of the central carbide, answer a question that no earlier prize has addressed: what the metal cluster that breaks the N2 triple bond looks like. The structures were determined rather than inferred, have been refined and independently confirmed over three decades, and anchor all later spectroscopic and computational work on the enzyme. That is a clean and defensible achievement in the sense the committee has traditionally used, and it can be stated in physical and chemical terms without claiming a catalytic cycle we do not yet have. In round 1 I proposed Rees, Einsle and Seefeldt under a 'structure and mechanism' citation. Having read Dr. Zou's reply, I think that wording promised more than the evidence supports, and that if the citation is about structure, Seefeldt's kinetic and spectroscopic contribution is the part that falls outside it.
statement.case_against: The mechanism is unresolved, so the citation must stay on structure and composition. Even then, credit is not simple: Dean's genetics and biochemistry and Ribbe's cofactor chemistry are real contributions, and Seefeldt's kinetic framework is what most of the field uses to interpret turnover. A two-name structure citation leaves all three out, and an expert report must tell us whether that omission can be defended. No other member ranked B064 first, so I cannot claim broad support. Finally, the committee must decide whether a structure of a known enzyme counts as a chemical discovery or as structural biology that the field accepted slowly.

responses.point: Nitrogenase should be limited to the cofactor structure, naming Rees and Einsle, with the exclusion of Dean, Seefeldt and Ribbe as an uncomfortable cost; Zou pairs it with a Liu-only base-editing part.
responses.response: On the chair's question, yes: I now agree with a citation limited to the structure of the enzyme and the cofactor, and I have dropped Seefeldt from my set, so that Rees and Einsle are our common core. Your question about how the kinetics could be split is fair. My answer is that they should not be folded into the citation at all, and that the expert report should state why Dean, Seefeldt and Ribbe fall outside a structure-centred prize. I do not follow you into the pairing with base editing. A second part chosen mainly because it has broad support is the kind of count-driven reasoning I would avoid. I would take a single-part prize on its merits.

responses.point: Base editing is a conceptually simple, widely reproduced and clinically used game-changer that is chemistry in the strict sense, now credited to Liu alone; the tunnelling picture of Gray and Winkler rests on Marcus theory, honoured in 1992.
responses.response: Your point about Marcus theory is a fair one and I have lowered B060 to a fallback. Gray and Winkler's quantitative contribution, the distance and driving-force dependence in proteins, is real, but how much of it is theirs rather than Dutton and Moser's is not something I can settle from memory. On base editing I accept that Liu alone is the cleanest attribution and that the adenine editor required real protein evolution. I still need the expert report to say what chemical principle is new beyond a deaminase fused to a CRISPR scaffold that the Academy recognised in 2020. Off-target deamination data are also still accumulating, and I would not call that maturity complete.

responses.point: Targeted protein degradation turns the ubiquitin-proteasome system into designable chemistry, with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli as a trio and many degraders in clinical trials; the credit boundary with the cereblon strand is acknowledged.
responses.response: I take your point that a confirmed mechanism matters more than an approval, and that the ternary-complex chemistry is quantitative. My reservation is the one you list yourself: PROTAC and cereblon-glue work have different discoverers, and the committee would have to pick one strand. The thalidomide mechanism explains a drug that has been used for decades, so a PROTAC-only citation risks the appearance of passing over the discovery that explains an existing drug class. I do not see that resolved by round 2. If the expert report can delimit the principle cleanly, I would regard the field as a strong candidate in a later year.

responses.point: Nanopore sensing rests on a single physical principle and is mature, with Deamer, Bayley and Akeson as the proposed laureates; Branton and Kasianowicz are left out.
responses.response: I agree with you on the principle, and ionic-current transduction in a single-molecule channel is a physical mechanism I find convincing. The attribution remains my difficulty: the first translocation experiments (Kasianowicz, Branton, Deamer) and the later enabling steps (Bayley's engineered pores, Akeson's ratchet) cannot be separated without a priority judgement the committee has not yet made. I would put B003 close behind B064 and would move toward it if the report supports a cut that Branton and Kasianowicz would accept. The same Branton and Kasianowicz problem keeps me from ranking it first.

responses.point: Pd-catalysed C-N coupling is the clearest general synthetic method, paired with a Crews-only degrader credit to keep the union at three people.
responses.response: I accept that C-N coupling is mature and that it extends the ligand logic of 2010 in a real way. I do not think a Crews-only credit is defensible, as you note yourself, and a two-part prize built to fit the three-person limit makes the Kosugi/Migita priority question and the 2010 overlap harder to defend, not easier. I would put C-N coupling after nitrogenase because the earlier prize already recognised the core principle.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports will support leaving Dean, Seefeldt and Ribbe out of a structure-only citation, or whether the committee must widen it.
Whether a citation limited to the cofactor structure is a chemical discovery or structural biology that the committee will not regard as a prize-level discovery.
Whether Gray and Winkler's contribution to electron tunnelling in proteins is distinct from Marcus theory and from the Dutton and Moser work.
Whether the committee will accept base editing as distinct from the 2020 CRISPR prize, and how the Kondo and Nishida priority claim is resolved.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific conflict, and no recusal is needed. I remain a Stockholm University colleague of Dr. Zou, who also supports nitrogenase, and I have not coordinated my view with him. My own field, respiratory-chain electron and proton transfer, is adjacent to B060 and B064, and I flag that I am judging neighbouring areas. This is unchanged from round 1.
